content: Dysfunctional breathing is characterized by chronic or recurrent alterations in breathing patterns, leading to both respiratory and non-respiratory symptoms. This term includes conditions such as hyperventilation syndrome and vocal cord dysfunction. It is estimated to affect approximately 10% of the general population. Common symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnoea), chest tightness, frequent sighing, and chest pain, all of which are linked to changes in respiratory patterns and rates. In children, dysfunctional breathing is not well understood. Preliminary data suggest that at least 5.3% of children with asthma may also have dysfunctional breathing. Unlike adults, children with this condition appear to experience poorer asthma control. However, the prevalence of dysfunctional breathing in the general pediatric population remains unknown. While breathing retraining is recommended as a first-line treatment for adults with dysfunctional breathing (with or without asthma), there are no established guidelines for managing this condition in children. Consequently, breathing retraining for children is often adapted from adult protocols, taking into account the child’s age and developmental abilities. The primary objectives of this review were to assess whether breathing retraining in children with dysfunctional breathing improves quality of life and to determine whether such interventions have any adverse effects. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using electronic databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as other resources like the National Research Register Archive and the Current Controlled Trials register. The most recent search was completed in October 2013. The inclusion criteria for this review were strict. Only randomized, quasi-randomized, or cluster-randomized controlled trials were considered. Observational studies, case studies, and cross-over design studies were excluded, as the long-lasting effects of breathing retraining could confound results in cross-over designs. Eligible participants were children up to 18 years of age with a clinical diagnosis of dysfunctional breathing. Children with asthma were included, with plans for subgroup analysis, but those with symptoms due to cardiac or metabolic diseases were excluded. The review considered any type of breathing retraining exercise, such as breathing control, diaphragmatic breathing, yoga breathing, Buteyko breathing, biofeedback-guided breathing modification, and techniques to suppress yawning or sighing. Both supervised and unsupervised programs were eligible, as were interventions incorporating relaxation techniques or acute episode management, provided breathing exercises were a core component. Interventions without a focus on breathing exercises were excluded. Data extraction was planned to be conducted independently by two authors, with discrepancies resolved by consensus or by consulting a third author if necessary. However, despite identifying 264 potential studies, only 224 unique papers remained after removing duplicates. Of these, six full-text articles were reviewed in detail, but none met the inclusion criteria. As a result, no studies were included in this systematic review. The authors concluded that the lack of suitable trials means this review cannot provide evidence to guide clinical practice. It remains unclear whether breathing retraining offers benefits for children with dysfunctional breathing or whether specific types of breathing exercises are more effective than others. Given the frequent use of breathing exercises to manage dysfunctional breathing and hyperventilation syndrome, there is an urgent need for well-designed clinical trials in this area. Future research should adhere to the CONSORT guidelines for reporting standards, use validated outcome measures, and ensure complete disclosure of data for all clinically relevant outcomes.
